questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Developer role from the Platform App Builder role, per Lesson 1's five Salesforce ecosystem roles?
options: A Developer extends the platform programmatically with Apex and Lightning Web Components; a Platform App Builder designs and deploys full custom applications using only declarative tools, without writing code.
A Developer extends the platform programmatically with Apex and Lightning Web Components; a Platform App Builder also writes Apex, but only for simple validation logic.
A Platform App Builder configures security and automation declaratively; a Developer only writes front-end code and never touches Apex.
Both roles do the exact same work in practice; "Platform App Builder" is simply an older name the ecosystem used for the Developer role.
A Developer is the entry point into the Salesforce ecosystem, and a Platform App Builder is a more senior role every developer eventually becomes.

A Platform App Builder manages org-wide architecture decisions across multiple connected clouds and integration patterns, while a Developer, by contrast, only ever works within the boundaries of a single custom object and never touches security at all.
questions.explain: Platform App Builder extends the Administrator skill set into designing and deploying full custom applications using the platform's declarative tools, without writing code. A Developer is the role that reaches for Apex and Lightning Web Components once declarative tools hit their limit.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the closest wrong answer because it correctly describes the Developer half, but then claims a Platform App Builder also writes Apex — it doesn't. Platform App Builder is specifically the declarative, no-code extension of the Administrator role; writing Apex at all, even for simple logic, is what pushes a task into the Developer role instead.

questions.prompt: Which resume bullet below correctly follows the action + artifact + tool pattern from Lesson 2?
options: Built a 5-step Record-Triggered Flow that auto-assigns new Leads by territory and SLA, replacing a manual queue-triage process.
Worked on automating our sales process.
Helped with reporting for the sales team.
Was responsible for various Salesforce administration duties.
questions.explain: The action + artifact + tool pattern names a real number, a real deliverable, and the real Salesforce tool used to build it. "Built a 5-step Record-Triggered Flow that auto-assigns new Leads by territory and SLA" names all three; the other options are exactly the vague, generic phrasing Lesson 2 warns against.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Trailhead profiles, ranks, and Superbadges, per Lesson 3.
options: A public Trailhead profile makes your learning activity checkable, but doesn't by itself prove on-the-job experience.
A high Trailblazer Rank is a relevance signal — the higher the rank, the more qualified you are for any specific role.
A Superbadge is harder to fake than an ordinary badge, because it's a hands-on, scenario-based challenge graded against a real org.
A Trail is a guided sequence of badges built around one specific role or skill.
Setting a Trailhead profile to Public reveals your login credentials to anyone with the link.
questions.explain: A public profile makes learning activity checkable, not on-the-job experience. Rank is a volume signal, not a relevance signal — a Double Star Ranger with no relevant trails isn't more hireable than a Hiker with the right Superbadge. A Superbadge is graded hands-on against a real org, which is what makes it hard to fake, and a Trail is a guided, role-specific badge sequence. Public visibility never exposes login credentials.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a ________ is a longer, hands-on, scenario-based Trailhead challenge where you're given a business problem and must actually build the solution in a real org, with the platform checking your work — making it the strongest signal on a profile short of an earned certification.
questions.explain: A Superbadge can't be passed by memorizing answers the way an ordinary badge's quiz can — it's a hands-on challenge graded against a real org, which is exactly what makes it the strongest signal short of an actual earned certification.

questions.prompt: Match each source-driven development term to what it actually is, per Lesson 5.
right: A temporary, disposable Salesforce org created from source for development and testing
The current Salesforce CLI command set, successor to the retired sfdx v7 prefix
The config file marking a directory as a Salesforce DX project
Treating local, version-controlled files, not the org, as the source of truth
questions.explain: Source-driven development treats local files as the source of truth. sf is the current CLI, replacing the retired sfdx v7 prefix. sfdx-project.json is the config file marking a DX project. A scratch org is a temporary, disposable org created from that source.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of getting a capstone's metadata into a GitHub-ready, source-driven project, per Lesson 5, in the correct order.
items: Authenticate the CLI against your org with sf org login web
Generate a new source-driven project with sf template generate project
Pull existing metadata from the org into local source with sf project retrieve start
Commit the source-formatted metadata to Git, excluding the .sfdx and .sf auth directories
questions.explain: The CLI has to be installed and authenticated before any project exists, a source-driven project has to be generated before metadata can land in it, and metadata has to be retrieved from the org before there's anything real to commit — with auth directories excluded the entire time.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes certification sequencing, per Lesson 7?
options: Each Salesforce credential assumes the skills of the ones that typically come before it, so jumping straight to an advanced exam without that foundation usually means either failing it or passing it without actually being able to do the job.
Each Salesforce credential assumes the skills of the ones before it, except Platform App Builder, which can be taken with no Administrator background at all.
Certification order doesn't really matter, since Salesforce designs every exam to be equally approachable regardless of prior credentials.
Only the Architect domain credentials have any prerequisites; Administrator and Platform App Builder can be taken in either order.

Passing an advanced exam without the right foundation guarantees, in every single case and without any possible exception whatsoever, that you will eventually fail at the actual on-the-job responsibilities the credential is supposed to represent.
Certification sequencing is only a suggestion from this course, not something reflected in Salesforce's own credential structure.
questions.explain: Each credential assumes the skills typically built by the ones before it — the Platform App Builder exam assumes Administrator-level comfort with objects, fields, and security, and the Architect domain credentials assume real Developer and Administrator depth. Skipping the foundation tends to end in failing the exam, or passing it without being able to actually do the job.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the closest wrong answer because it restates the correct general rule, then carves out a false exception for Platform App Builder — the lesson is explicit that Platform App Builder assumes Administrator-level comfort with objects, fields, and security, with no stated exception. That invented carve-out is the error.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 8, why does rebuilding a weak exam topic hands-on in a Trailhead Playground teach you something a practice exam question can't?
options: A practice question only tests whether you can recognize the right answer among choices; rebuilding it hands-on proves you can actually configure the thing yourself, without a guide open.
Practice exams are always factually inaccurate, so hands-on practice is the only reliable source of truth about exam content.
Hands-on practice is required because Trailhead only allows a practice assessment to be taken a single time.
There's no real difference between the two methods — both test the exact same underlying skill equally well.
questions.explain: A passed practice exam shows you can recognize the right answer on a quiz. Rebuilding a weak topic hands-on, with no guide open, is the only way to confirm you can actually do the configuration — which is the real readiness check Lesson 8 describes.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 9, select every Architect domain credential confirmed as currently live on Trailhead's catalog.
options: Data Architect
Sharing and Visibility Architect
Integration Architect
Identity and Access Management Architect
Email Marketing Architect
Flow Automation Architect
questions.explain: Lesson 9 names Data Architect, Sharing and Visibility Architect, Integration Architect, and Identity and Access Management Architect as confirmed, currently live Architect domain credentials. "Email Marketing Architect" and "Flow Automation Architect" aren't credentials the lesson names at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: before registering for any Salesforce certification exam, Lesson 10's checklist says to go directly to trailhead.salesforce.com/credentials and read the current ________ in full — objectives, prerequisites, question format, time limit, and passing score — rather than trusting a course, blog, or older material.
questions.explain: The exam guide is the credential's official, current objectives, prerequisites, and format, published and maintained directly by Salesforce — the one source Lesson 10 says should override anything read elsewhere, including this course.

questions.prompt: A user says they can't see a record they should be able to see. Per Lesson 11, which order should you actually troubleshoot this in?
options: Object and field-level access first, then org-wide defaults, then role hierarchy and sharing rules, then manual or Apex-managed sharing.
Manual sharing first, since it's the most specific exception, then work backward to org-wide defaults last.
Role hierarchy first, since it's the most commonly misconfigured layer, then everything else in any order.
Check org-wide defaults only — the other layers rarely matter in a real troubleshooting scenario.
questions.explain: Lesson 11's layered order starts with whether the user can touch the object at all (profile, permission sets), then the baseline visibility (org-wide defaults), then what's been granted on top of that (role hierarchy and sharing rules), then the most specific, most recently-added exceptions (manual or Apex-managed sharing).

questions.prompt: A trigger runs a SOQL query inside a for loop, once per record being processed. It passes every sandbox test run against one record at a time. What happens when 200 records are updated at once via Data Loader, per Lesson 12?
options: It's very likely to fail in production by hitting a governor limit, because the query now runs once per record in the batch instead of once total.
It will run exactly the same way it did with one record, because governor limits only ever apply to DML, never to SOQL.
Salesforce automatically batches the trigger into groups of one record each, so the loop never actually executes more than once.
It fails immediately at save time with a syntax error, regardless of how many records are in the batch.
questions.explain: This is the classic non-bulkified trigger bug: a query per record inside a loop works fine with one record and then fails in production the first time a batch of 200 arrives, because governor limits cap synchronous SOQL query count per transaction, not per record.

questions.prompt: A client asks for something that would break a Salesforce best practice. Per Lesson 13, what's the strongest way to respond?
options: Acknowledge the request, explain the specific downside in terms the client cares about (cost, risk, maintainability), and offer an alternative that gets them most of what they actually need.
Simply tell them it's against best practice and decline to build it.
Build exactly what they asked for without comment, since the client is always the final authority on Salesforce design.
Escalate the request to Salesforce support for an official ruling before responding to the client at all.
questions.explain: Saying "that's against best practice" without translating the tradeoff into terms the client cares about reads as rigid, not expert. The stronger answer names the real downside and offers an alternative that still gets the client most of what they need.

questions.prompt: Select every behavior Lesson 14 recommends when working through an open-ended Architect scenario interview.
options: Ask clarifying questions first, since real requirements are almost always incomplete on purpose.
State your assumptions out loud when a clarifying question doesn't get fully answered.
Jump straight to naming a specific product feature before confirming the actual business constraint.
Propose a direction with the tradeoffs named explicitly, rather than one confident answer with no tradeoffs.
Avoid mentioning security or large-data-volume considerations unless the interviewer asks about them directly.
questions.explain: Lesson 14 recommends clarifying first, stating assumptions out loud, and naming tradeoffs explicitly. Jumping to a feature name before understanding the constraint, and skipping security or scale unless asked, are exactly the weak-answer patterns the lesson warns against.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 15, why is narrating continuously while you draw a whiteboard design stronger than drawing in silence and explaining afterward?
options: Silence while drawing reads as uncertainty even when you're confident, while narrating keeps the room oriented to your reasoning as it develops.
Narrating is required because whiteboard markers in most interview rooms don't actually work well enough to draw complex diagrams.
It has no real effect on how the panel perceives you — only the finished diagram is ever actually evaluated.
Narrating lets you skip labeling your boxes and arrows, since you're explaining them out loud instead.
questions.explain: The whiteboard is graded alongside the architecture itself. Explaining as you draw, instead of after, keeps the panel following your reasoning in real time — silence reads as uncertainty even when the design in your head is correct.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 16, why should you prepare three different versions of the same capstone presentation instead of one version for every audience?
options: A recruiter, a hiring manager, and a technical panel want different levels of detail, and using the wrong depth for the wrong audience either wastes limited time or reads as unprepared.
Salesforce requires a different presentation format depending on which interview round you're in.
Only the technical-panel version is ever actually used; the recruiter and hiring-manager versions exist purely as backups.
Recruiters and hiring managers are not allowed to hear any technical detail at all, by policy.
questions.explain: A recruiter wants the business problem and outcome in under a minute. A hiring manager wants decisions and tradeoffs. A technical panel wants the actual detail. Using the technical-panel version on a recruiter screen wastes limited time; using the recruiter version on a panel reads as unprepared.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks why you used a permission set instead of creating a new profile. Per Lesson 17's option/reason/cost framework, which answer demonstrates the strongest reasoning?
options: A permission set lets you grant additional access without creating a new profile for every access combination, which avoids profile sprawl — though it does add one more layer to audit.
A permission set is best practice, so that's what I used.
I used a permission set because profiles can't grant any additional access beyond what a permission set already provides.
There's no real cost to using a permission set instead of a profile — it's strictly better in every single situation.
questions.explain: "Best practice" names a conclusion, not a reason. The strongest answer names what was chosen, the actual tradeoff it resolves (avoiding profile sprawl), and the real cost it still carries (one more layer to audit) — exactly the option/reason/cost structure Lesson 17 teaches.

questions.prompt: Select every statement below that describes a recommended practice during a new Salesforce hire's first 90 days, per Lesson 18 — not a common mistake to avoid.
options: Changing production directly because sandbox testing felt unnecessary for something small.
Studying the real data model and existing security setup before changing anything, in the first 30 days.
Trying to re-architect the entire org in week one.
Delivering a small, well-scoped win between days 30 and 60 to build trust.
Going quiet instead of asking why something works the way it does.
questions.explain: Studying the existing data model and security setup before changing anything, and delivering a small, well-scoped win once you understand the org, are the recommended arc. Changing production directly, re-architecting everything in week one, and going quiet instead of asking are the explicit mistakes Lesson 18 warns against.

questions.prompt: Put these milestones toward Certified Technical Architect (CTA), per Lesson 19, in the correct order.
items: Salesforce Certified Administrator, then Salesforce Certified Platform App Builder
Architect domain credentials (data, sharing and visibility, integration, identity and access management, development lifecycle and deployment)
Architect milestones: Application Architect and System Architect
Salesforce Certified Technical Architect (CTA), earned through a review-board process
questions.explain: The Technical Architect ladder builds in layers: the Administrator and Platform App Builder foundation, then Platform Developer I, then the Architect domain credentials, bundled into the Application Architect and System Architect milestones, and finally CTA itself through a review-board process.

questions.prompt: An interviewer asks what you'd do differently about a design decision in your capstone. Per Lesson 17, what's the correct way to understand this question?
options: It's a question about scale and hindsight — what assumption held true at the size you built it, but would start to strain at ten times the size — not an invitation to confess a mistake.
It's a trap designed to get you to admit the entire design was wrong from the start.
It only applies if you actually made an error, so if you didn't, the honest answer is simply "nothing."
It's testing whether you'll change your answer to agree with whatever the interviewer suggests next.
questions.explain: The question is about scale and hindsight, not a confession. A strong answer treats it as a continuation of the tradeoff framework — "at this scale, X was the right tradeoff; past a certain point, I'd reconsider it because Y" — rather than backing away from the original decision.
